strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer-vision problem: transferring time-varying effects from a reference video while preserving a separate input video's content and motion. Reference conditioning is well motivated for effects that are difficult to specify precisely through text.

The strongest contribution is the complementary data construction pipeline. Combining LoRA-generated I2V examples, pose-aligned V2V synthesis, and programmatic effects provides a practical route to training triplets that are otherwise difficult to obtain. This is valuable under the default Algorithms/General assessment even though the architecture largely extends existing conditioning mechanisms.

The conditioning design is straightforward and technically plausible. Figure 5 explains how input and reference latents enter the pretrained diffusion transformer, and the framework supports both image and video inputs without per-reference optimization.

The reported human preferences and qualitative examples provide encouraging evidence of useful transfer. Reference-adherence preferences favor RefVFX across all three evaluation settings, and the no-reference ablation provides some evidence that the reference contributes beyond the text prompt.

The supplement candidly identifies occlusion failures, human-centric training coverage, and computational cost. It also provides effect libraries, parameter ranges, and inference settings that help characterize the contribution.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not convincingly isolate temporal-effect transfer from reference appearance or semantic similarity. VideoPrism similarity can reward transferring reference content without accurately reproducing effect timing. Figure 8 explicitly shows reference clothing becoming more influential with increased guidance. Temporal-order controls, matched references with different timing, or comparisons against a static reference would better substantiate the central disentanglement claim. Programmatic effects also offer an opportunity for exact target-based evaluation that is not used.

The human study is the principal evidence, but essential protocol details are missing from the supplied supplement: participant count, comparisons per example, randomization, instructions, tie handling, and uncertainty estimates. In particular, the no-reference comparisons report 81.5–93.6% win rates alongside mean advantages as small as +0.15 or +0.18. These can be compatible when ties are excluded, but the denominator and tie distribution must be specified to interpret the apparent strength of preference.

Comparisons and ablations leave the source of improvement uncertain. The external baselines receive text rather than reference videos, while the no-reference variant removes conditioning from the already trained model rather than establishing a matched text-only training baseline. There are no data-source ablations or static-reference controls. Despite claims about outperforming reference-guided methods, the experiments do not compare against such a method; the cited dynamic-concept approaches would be relevant at least for the overlapping I2V setting.

Generalization claims exceed the demonstrated coverage. Code-based testing holds out parameter settings within training effect and transition families, rather than effect categories. Neural V2V testing uses novel prompts from the same generation pipeline without clearly documenting semantic separation, and the cross-domain subset is not reported separately. The 28 held-out I2V LoRAs are encouraging, but broader claims about arbitrary videos and unseen effect categories need more precise splits and subgroup results.

The dataset's scale and quality are insufficiently audited. Most of the claimed 1,700 effects are 1,500 parameterized programmatic compositions, which should be distinguished from distinct semantic categories. The neural V2V subset size, pair-alignment quality, filtering yield, and source-video disjointness are not clearly reported. Pose conditioning alone does not establish that generated pairs preserve background, identity, and non-pose motion.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: LoRA rank and target modules, learning rate, optimizer, exact conditioning-dropout probabilities, and guidance settings for the reported comparisons are unspecified. Architectural details promised in the supplement are also absent. Code release is promised, but dataset, split, and checkpoint availability are unclear, weakening the claimed benchmark contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: transferring temporally evolving visual effects from a reference video while preserving a separate input video's content and motion. Under the default Algorithms/General category, the task formulation and data pipeline are meaningful contributions even though the architecture largely extends existing components.

The three-source training pipeline is resourceful. Combining LoRA-generated effects, pose-conditioned video pairs, and programmatic effects provides complementary supervision. The first/last-frame and intermediate-pose construction is a practical approach to obtaining otherwise scarce paired training data.

The reported results are promising. Tables 1–2 show substantial human preference over text-conditioned baselines, and the inference-time No Ref ablation provides evidence that reference conditioning helps. Table 4 also shows improved reference similarity across both V2V settings.

The manuscript explains the overall pipeline clearly and provides useful effect catalogs and generation settings. The supplement candidly identifies occlusion failures, human-centric data coverage, and inference cost; these disclosures improve the assessment.
weaknesses: The principal evidence—the human study—is insufficiently specified. Although annotation totals are provided, the manuscript does not report participant counts, examples per comparison, assignment and randomization procedures, annotation filtering criteria, uncertainty, or how ties enter the win-rate denominator. This matters particularly for comparisons such as 92.9% wins but only +0.18 mean preference against No Ref. The promised supplementary study details are absent from the supplied PDF, making the magnitude and reliability of the main result difficult to assess.

The quantitative metrics do not establish the central claim of transferring temporal dynamics independently of reference content. Whole-video embedding similarity can reward shared appearance or semantic content without verifying transition timing, motion preservation, or avoidance of reference-content leakage. Neural V2V input similarity is also lower than both VACE variants (0.8568 versus 0.9068/0.9460). Under-editing is a plausible explanation, but these measurements cannot distinguish it from poorer preservation. Controlled temporal tests and evaluation against programmatically available targets would provide substantially stronger evidence.

The experiments do not adequately isolate the proposed mechanism and data contributions. No Ref removes conditioning at inference from the already trained model; there is no matched text-only training comparison, ablation of the three dataset sources, or static/shuffled-reference control. Consequently, the results leave unclear how much improvement comes from task-specific training and appearance cues versus learning the reference's temporal evolution. The conclusion also claims superiority over static-reference baselines without reporting such a comparison.

Generalization claims exceed the documented split design. Holding out 28 LoRA effects is useful, but novel V2V prompts do not necessarily imply unseen effect categories, and code-based evaluation explicitly reuses training effect families with different parameters. Exact category separation, source-video disjointness, and per-subset test counts are not sufficiently documented. These experiments support some transfer to unseen instances, but not the broad category-level generalization claimed throughout.

The dataset's quality and reproducibility are not adequately established relative to its central role. Pose conditioning alone does not guarantee preservation of background, identity, or detailed motion, yet there is no quantitative audit of generated pair alignment or effect consistency. The headline 1,700 effects also includes 1,500 parameterized programmatic compositions and should be distinguished from semantic effect categories. Exact split manifests, a complete LoRA inventory, and a clear dataset-release commitment are missing; the explicit release promise concerns code.

Important implementation details remain unspecified, including learning rate, optimizer, LoRA rank and target modules, conditioning-dropout probabilities, and the guidance settings used for reported comparisons. The supplement does not supply the promised conditioning and cross-attention details. These gaps, together with the evaluation concerns above, prevent a sufficiently convincing case for acceptance despite the promising task and pipeline.

strengths: RefVFX addresses a meaningful video-editing problem: transferring temporally evolving effects from a reference while preserving another video's content and motion. Reference videos offer useful control beyond textual effect descriptions.

The complementary data pipelines are a substantive contribution. Combining LoRA-generated effects, pose-conditioned video pairs, and programmatic effects provides a plausible, scalable approach to obtaining otherwise difficult training supervision.

The conditioning architecture is straightforward and technically plausible. It supports both image and video inputs without per-reference optimization, and separate guidance controls provide a useful mechanism for balancing input preservation and effect adherence.

The qualitative examples show promising temporal transformations, and the reported human preferences favor RefVFX across all three evaluated settings. Testing 28 held-out I2V LoRAs provides meaningful evidence beyond memorizing training effects.
The supplement candidly discusses occlusion failures, human-centric data coverage, and computational cost. These limitations help establish the practical scope of the contribution.
weaknesses: The central claim of transferring temporal dynamics is not adequately isolated. VideoPrism similarity can reward shared appearance or reference-content leakage without verifying effect timing or input-motion preservation. Table 4 also shows lower neural-V2V input similarity than both VACE variants. This could reflect appropriate editing, but the metrics cannot resolve that tradeoff. Temporally shuffled or static-reference controls, alongside timing-sensitive evaluation, would strengthen the scientific case.

The human study is the primary evidence, but its protocol is insufficiently documented. The manuscript reports annotation totals without participant counts, per-comparison sample sizes, randomization details, uncertainty estimates, or a clear treatment of ties. The 92.9% preference against No Ref with only a +0.18 mean score particularly needs explanation. The promised supplementary study details are absent from the supplied PDF.

Comparisons mainly establish an advantage over text-conditioned systems with less conditioning information. The No Ref test is useful but removes conditioning from the already-trained model rather than comparing against a separately trained, data-matched text-only model. Related reference-based dynamic-concept approaches are discussed but not experimentally compared, and the conclusion's claim of outperforming static-reference baselines is not supported by the listed experiments.

Generalization and dataset breadth require more precise characterization. The 1,500 programmatic effects are parameterized compositions, and their test set uses the same operation and transition families with unseen parameters. Novel V2V prompts likewise do not necessarily establish unseen semantic categories. Exact split sizes, semantic overlap checks, and data-source ablations are missing, leaving uncertainty about which data contributions enable transfer.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful implementation details: LoRA rank, learning rate, exact conditioning-dropout probabilities, and quantitative-test guidance settings are unspecified. Dataset counts do not clearly distinguish generated clips from sampled triplets, and dataset release is not clearly committed to despite the benchmark claim. Overall, the task and results are promising, but the evaluation and attribution gaps leave a slight preference for rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer-vision problem: transferring temporally evolving effects from a reference video while preserving another video's content and motion. Under Algorithms/General, the combined data-generation and modeling contribution supports a slight preference for acceptance, even though the architectural changes are relatively simple.

The three-source dataset is a substantial contribution. In particular, the neural V2V pipeline combines first/last-frame generation with intermediate pose conditioning to create approximately motion-aligned editing pairs. Programmatic effects provide complementary, precisely controlled temporal transformations.

The human evaluation provides meaningful support for practical effectiveness: over 15,000 annotations from over 500 annotators, randomized presentation, and bootstrap uncertainty estimates. Overall-match preferences consistently favor RefVFX, including against the same model without reference conditioning, with approximately 60–67% win rates.

Evaluation covers I2V, neural V2V, and programmatic V2V, including 28 held-out LoRA effects. Figures 6–7 illustrate plausible improvements in progressive transformations over text-conditioned baselines. The supplement also candidly documents occlusion failures, human-centric data coverage, and computational cost.
weaknesses: The evidence does not fully isolate transfer of temporal dynamics from transfer of appearance or semantics. VideoPrism reference similarity can increase through reference-content leakage, and the No Ref ablation only establishes the value of reference conditioning generally. Static-reference, shuffled-frame, or controlled timing comparisons would more directly test the central temporal-transfer claim. Programmatic effects also offer an opportunity for ground-truth timing and localization evaluation that is not used.

Generalization claims exceed the precision of the reported splits. Programmatic testing holds out hyperparameters rather than effect families; novel neural-effect prompts do not necessarily establish unseen semantic categories. Exact V2V subset sizes, source-video separation, effect overlap, and manual-filtering criteria are missing. Thus, generalization to genuinely new effect categories is less established than generalization to new instances.

The contribution of each training source is not measured. Without source-removal experiments or a quality audit of generated pairs, it is unclear how much the proposed neural V2V pipeline contributes beyond LoRA and programmatic data. Pose conditioning alone does not guarantee preservation of background, identity, camera motion, or fine geometry.

The strongest conclusions about preservation and statistical reliability need qualification. For neural V2V, input similarity is 0.8568 versus 0.9460 for VACE Depth; this may reflect necessary editing, but the metric cannot establish that explanation. Some human-study preservation results, such as 51.3 ± 3.1% against No Ref, are compatible with chance. Appendix E's adjacent-frame CLIP similarity also does not directly establish motion smoothness and can reward static outputs.

Reproducibility and positioning remain incomplete. The manuscript omits learning rate, LoRA rank and target modules, exact conditioning-dropout probabilities, and evaluation guidance settings. It promises code but does not clearly commit to releasing the claimed dataset/benchmark. Related dynamic-concept methods are discussed without experimental comparison, particularly relevant for I2V. Finally, seven minutes for a 33-frame clip limits the efficiency claim: tuning-free inference is demonstrated, but fast generation is not.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer-vision problem: transferring temporally evolving effects from a reference video while preserving another video's content and motion. Reference-based control is well motivated for effects that are difficult to specify precisely through text.

The data construction is a substantive contribution. Combining LoRA-generated effects, pose-aligned video pairs, and programmatic temporal transformations provides a plausible, scalable route to supervision. The endpoint-editing and intermediate-pose pipeline is particularly useful.

The human evaluation provides meaningful positive evidence: over 15,000 annotations from over 500 annotators, randomized presentation, practice trials, and bootstrap uncertainty estimates. Overall-match preferences are approximately 60–67% against the tested baselines, with improvements also over the No Ref ablation.

Figures 6–7 illustrate convincing examples of progressive transformations, and the supplementary material acknowledges failures involving occlusion, human-centric data coverage, and computational cost. Training scale, inference settings, effect parameter ranges, and principal data sources are documented.
weaknesses: The central claim of transferring reference-specific temporal dynamics is insufficiently isolated. Removing reference conditioning shows that references help, but there are no static-frame, repeated-frame, temporally shuffled, or reversed-reference controls. Consequently, the experiments do not establish how much improvement comes from temporal information rather than appearance or semantic cues. Controlled tests varying reference timing while holding content and text fixed would directly address this.

The quantitative metrics do not resolve this concern. VideoPrism similarity to the reference can reward shared content or appearance without establishing faithful effect timing, and input similarity does not directly measure motion preservation. Section 4.4 reports no ground-truth evaluation, although the programmatic pipeline could generate exact targets. Appendix E's adjacent-frame CLIP similarity likewise cannot establish motion smoothness reliably. The human study supports perceptual usefulness, but the stronger temporal-coherence claims remain under-validated.

Generalization is described more broadly than the splits demonstrate. Unseen LoRAs, unseen prompts, and unseen programmatic hyperparameters represent different forms of novelty; the latter does not establish unseen effect-category generalization. The V2V test set is described only as over 100 instances, without exact source counts, complete held-out effect lists, or per-category results. This makes the breadth and difficulty of generalization hard to assess.

The data and architectural contributions lack targeted ablations. There are no experiments removing individual data sources or comparing conditioning designs, and it is unclear whether No Ref is independently trained or simply evaluated with reference conditioning dropped. All external quantitative baselines are text-conditioned; the related dynamic-concept methods cited in Section 2 are not experimentally compared, even on compatible I2V cases. Thus, the evidence establishes an advantage over the selected prompt-based systems more clearly than over alternative reference-based approaches.

Reproducibility remains incomplete for a contribution centered on a new dataset and trained model. Learning rate, optimizer, LoRA rank and target modules, exact conditioning-dropout probabilities, and detailed split construction are missing. The headline counts mix clips, effect configurations, and triplets without a complete accounting of the neural V2V subset. Code release is promised, but dataset and checkpoint availability are not clearly committed.

Some conclusions overstate the evidence: for example, neural V2V input adherence against No Ref is 51.3 ± 3.1%, which does not establish a reliable preference despite the blanket statistical-reliability claim. Overall, the useful data pipeline and positive human results make this a close decision, but the missing temporal controls and incomplete generalization analysis lead to a slight preference for rejection under Algorithms/General.

strengths: Assessed as Algorithms/General, the paper addresses a useful computer-vision problem: transferring temporally evolving effects from a reference video while retaining another video's content and motion. The contribution combines task formulation, training-data construction, and reference-conditioned generation; its value does not depend on a fundamentally new diffusion architecture.

The data-generation pipeline is a substantive contribution. Combining LoRA-generated effects, pose-aligned video pairs, and programmatic temporal transformations provides a practical route to training supervision that is otherwise difficult to obtain. The first/last-frame and intermediate-pose construction is particularly useful.

The human evaluation provides meaningful evidence of effectiveness: over 15,000 annotations from over 500 annotators, randomized presentation, practice trials, and bootstrap uncertainty estimates. Overall-match preferences are approximately 60–67% across the reported comparisons. Improvements over the No Ref variant help establish the usefulness of reference conditioning beyond comparisons with off-the-shelf models.

Figures 6–7 illustrate convincing advantages for progressive transformations and effect timing. Evaluation includes 28 held-out I2V LoRA effects and real input videos, while the supplement candidly identifies occlusion failures, human-centric coverage, and computational cost. Together, these merits support a slight preference for acceptance.
weaknesses: The experiments only partially establish transfer of temporal dynamics independently of reference content. VideoPrism reference similarity can reward shared appearance or semantic content without demonstrating correct effect timing, and input similarity does not directly measure motion preservation. Reference-frame shuffling, static-reference conditioning, or controlled timing changes would better test the central temporal-transfer claim. The human study is valuable but does not resolve this mechanism question.

Generalization claims exceed the precision of the evaluation protocol. The code-based test uses unseen hyperparameters rather than clearly unseen effect families, and novel neural-effect prompts need not imply novel semantic categories. The manuscript reports only 'over 100' V2V validation instances without exact subset sizes or a complete train/test effect inventory. Since 1,500 of the advertised effects are programmatic compositions, the distinction between effect families and parameterized instances matters.

Ablations are limited to dropping the reference condition. There is no isolation of the three training sources, the custom V2V generation pipeline, or conditioning/mask design. The No Ref experiment appears to remove conditioning from the same trained model rather than compare against a separately trained, data-matched text-only editor. Comparisons also omit the related reference-based dynamic-concept methods discussed in Section 2, leaving the relative contribution of training data and architecture uncertain.

Several conclusions are overstated. Preference estimates such as 51.3 ± 3.1% for neural-V2V input adherence do not establish a reliable improvement over chance. Table 10 also shows mixed quality metrics rather than uniform superiority. These points warrant narrower claims, although the stronger overall-match preferences remain persuasive.

Reproducibility and practical scope need clarification. The supplement does not supply the promised precise conditioning-dropout settings, and learning rate, optimizer, LoRA rank, and exact dataset/split accounting are missing. Code release is promised, but dataset and benchmark release commitments are unclear. Experiments cover only 33 frames at 480p, requiring about seven minutes per output on an A100; 'tuning-free' appropriately means no per-example optimization, but broader efficiency and arbitrary-video claims should be qualified.
